thread.title: Samsung Highlights Artificial Intelligence, Cooperation at Electronics Show

title: Samsung Highlights Artificial Intelligence, Cooperation at Electronics Show
text:
Samsung Highlights Artificial Intelligence, Cooperation at Electronics Show By Jan. 8, 2019 10:55 a.m. ET Order Reprints Courtesy of Samsung Text size
If Samsung Electronics taught us anything at its product extravaganza at the Consumer Electronics Show late Monday, it’s that artificial intelligence is the glue that binds its vast array of products, and that it never hurts to cooperate with a fierce rival.
AI is the connective tissue among a slew of smart home appliances, a digital car cockpit, and robots it showcased on a massive stage containing a smart refrigerator, oven, dish washer and dryer, and big-screen TV. They, and a smart-car system, performed tasks –often at the same time–through commands via Samsung’s Bixby voice assistant.
“AI is integral to our vision of the future,” Samsung Chief Executive HS Kim said. He and a team of company executives also confirmed Samsung will release a 5G-ready smartphone this year, and introduced robots as an extension of its home appliances. (The home robot could conceivably morph into a vacuum or lawn mower.)
Artificial intelligence and fast connectivity are expected to push the U.S. consumer tech industry to a record $398 billion in retail sales in 2019, up 3.9% from 2018, according to a forecast by the Consumer Technology Association. Newsletter Sign-up
Samsung’s (ticker: South Korea: 005930) AI approach fits with its “kitchen-sink” product line–it makes everything from its own chips and smartphones to home appliances, and software and services —allowing it to interconnect them seamlessly. The company’s open platform also enables it to dive into fledgling markets such as internet of Things, smart homes, and 5G without missing a beat.
“We believe in consumers and their experiences. It’s stupid to exclude them” with closed computing environments, Samsung Senior Vice President Yoon Lee told Barron’s , in an apparent allusion to Apple ’s (AAPL) “walled garden” business model.
Samsung’s smartphone rival, which soared for more than a decade off the success of its iPhone franchise, is now experiencing the pain of a dip in iPhone sales , triggering a steep decline in its stock price. Although Samsung warned late Monday of worse-than-expected results, its stock held up better than Apple’s.
The rivalry doesn’t mean that Samsung and Apple can’t work together. Quite the contrary. The companies announced Monday that Samsung will offer iTunes for movies and TV shows on its smart TVs, and let AirPlay stream content from Apple devices to Samsung televisions.
Samsung’s co-opetition with Apple through iTunes, and separate partnerships with Alphabet’s (GOOGL) Google Assistant, and Amazon.com ’s (AMZN) Alexa “comes from the realization by everyone that walled gardens don’t maximize business opportunities,” Patrick Moorhead, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, told Barron’s .
